note: Angles for PSLE. Every fact carries the exact reason wording, a diagram, the clue that tells you to reach for it, and the trap.

discipline.title: Every step needs a reason
points: An angle question is not arithmetic. It is a short argument. Each line of working must say WHY, not just what.
Write the reason in brackets after every step: 62 degrees (vertically opposite angles). Marks are given for the reason as well as the number.
Never measure the diagram. PSLE diagrams are deliberately not to scale, and a figure that looks like a right angle usually is not one.
If you cannot see the answer, mark on the diagram every angle you CAN find, even the ones you do not need. The path usually appears once three or four are filled in.
Look for the shape the rule lives in: an F, a Z, a C, a triangle, a straight line. The letters are how the rule is spotted at speed.

facts.name: Angles on a straight line
facts.rule: Angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees.
facts.spot: Two or more angles sitting side by side along one straight edge.
clue: a straight line through a point
facts.trap: Only counts if the outer arms really do form one straight line. A line with a small kink is not a straight line.

facts.name: Angles at a point
facts.rule: Angles all the way round a point add up to 360 degrees.
facts.spot: Three or more angles meeting at one point with no straight line through it.
facts.trap: Students often use 180 out of habit. Check whether the arms close all the way round or only cover a half turn.

facts.name: Vertically opposite angles
facts.rule: When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal.
facts.spot: An X. The two angles facing each other across the crossing point.
facts.trap: Opposite means across the crossing point, not next to it. The two angles next to each other add to 180 instead.
facts.svg: <line x1='20' y1='30' x2='200' y2='130' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='20' y1='130' x2='200' y2='30' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><text x='104' y='58' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='13'>a</text><text x='104' y='118' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='13'>a</text><text x='62' y='90' fill='#f59e0b' font-size='13'>b</text><text x='148' y='90' fill='#f59e0b' font-size='13'>b</text>

facts.name: Corresponding angles (the F)
facts.rule: When a line crosses two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.
facts.spot: An F shape, in any rotation, including backwards and upside down. Both angles sit in the same corner of their own crossing.
clue: arrows on two lines showing they are parallel
facts.trap: The two lines must be parallel, shown by matching arrowheads. Without arrows you cannot use this rule at all.
facts.svg: <line x1='15' y1='45' x2='205' y2='45' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='15' y1='110' x2='205' y2='110' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='55' y1='10' x2='165' y2='145' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='96,41 102,45 96,49' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><polyline points='96,106 102,110 96,114' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M 88 45 A 18 18 0 0 0 78 32' fill='none' stroke='#38bdf8' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 141 110 A 18 18 0 0 0 131 97' fill='none' stroke='#38bdf8' stroke-width='2'/><text x='66' y='38' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='12'>a</text><text x='119' y='103' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='12'>a</text>

facts.name: Alternate angles (the Z)
facts.rule: When a line crosses two parallel lines, alternate angles are equal.
facts.spot: A Z shape, in any rotation. Both angles are BETWEEN the parallel lines and on OPPOSITE sides of the crossing line.
clue: on opposite sides of the transversal
facts.trap: Both angles must be inside the pair of parallel lines. If one is outside, it is not an alternate pair.
facts.svg: <line x1='15' y1='45' x2='205' y2='45' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='15' y1='110' x2='205' y2='110' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='55' y1='10' x2='165' y2='145' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='96,41 102,45 96,49' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><polyline points='96,106 102,110 96,114' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M 96 45 A 18 18 0 0 1 88 60' fill='none' stroke='#22c55e' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 124 110 A 18 18 0 0 1 133 96' fill='none' stroke='#22c55e' stroke-width='2'/><text x='104' y='64' fill='#22c55e' font-size='12'>a</text><text x='110' y='100' fill='#22c55e' font-size='12'>a</text>

facts.name: Co-interior angles (the C)
facts.rule: When a line crosses two parallel lines, co-interior angles add up to 180 degrees.
facts.spot: A C or U shape. Both angles are BETWEEN the parallel lines and on the SAME side of the crossing line.
facts.trap: This is the only parallel-line rule where the angles ADD to 180 instead of being equal. Mixing it with alternate angles is the commonest error in the whole topic.
facts.svg: <line x1='15' y1='45' x2='205' y2='45' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='15' y1='110' x2='205' y2='110' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='55' y1='10' x2='165' y2='145' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='96,41 102,45 96,49' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><polyline points='96,106 102,110 96,114' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M 96 45 A 18 18 0 0 1 88 60' fill='none' stroke='#f472b6' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 133 96 A 18 18 0 0 1 124 110' fill='none' stroke='#f472b6' stroke-width='2'/><text x='104' y='64' fill='#f472b6' font-size='12'>a</text><text x='138' y='102' fill='#f472b6' font-size='12'>b</text><text x='20' y='140' fill='currentColor' font-size='11'>a + b = 180</text>

facts.name: Angle sum of a triangle
facts.rule: The three angles inside any triangle add up to 180 degrees.
facts.spot: Any closed three-sided shape, however squashed it looks.
clue: a triangle anywhere in the figure
two angles given inside a triangle
facts.trap: Works for every triangle, not only neat ones. Also, a triangle hidden inside a bigger figure still counts, so look for triangles that are not drawn separately.
facts.svg: <polygon points='35,125 190,125 90,25' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 55 125 A 20 20 0 0 0 47 111' fill='none' stroke='#38bdf8' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 170 125 A 20 20 0 0 1 176 113' fill='none' stroke='#38bdf8' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 82 43 A 20 20 0 0 0 101 45' fill='none' stroke='#38bdf8' stroke-width='2'/><text x='50' y='118' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='12'>a</text><text x='160' y='118' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='12'>b</text><text x='86' y='58' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='12'>c</text><text x='120' y='145' fill='currentColor' font-size='11'>a + b + c = 180</text>

facts.name: Exterior angle of a triangle
facts.rule: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
facts.spot: One side of a triangle carries on past a corner, making an angle outside the triangle.
clue: a side extended beyond the vertex
an angle sitting outside the triangle
facts.trap: The two angles you add are the two you do NOT touch, that is the two at the far corners. Adding the neighbouring one is wrong.

facts.name: Isosceles triangle
facts.rule: In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal, because two sides are equal.
facts.reason: base angles of an isosceles triangle
facts.spot: Two sides marked with the same tick, or a problem that tells you two sides are equal.
clue: matching tick marks on two sides
facts.trap: The equal angles are the two OPPOSITE the equal sides, which are the base angles, not the apex. Also, a triangle folded inside a figure is often isosceles without being labelled.
facts.svg: <polygon points='45,125 175,125 110,30' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='72' y1='80' x2='82' y2='75' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='143' y1='75' x2='153' y2='80' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 65 125 A 20 20 0 0 0 58 110' fill='none' stroke='#22c55e' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 155 125 A 20 20 0 0 1 162 110' fill='none' stroke='#22c55e' stroke-width='2'/><text x='60' y='118' fill='#22c55e' font-size='12'>a</text><text x='152' y='118' fill='#22c55e' font-size='12'>a</text>

facts.name: Equilateral triangle
facts.rule: All three angles are 60 degrees, because all three sides are equal.
facts.spot: Three sides with matching ticks, or the word equilateral.
facts.trap: A triangle that looks equal is not equal. It must be marked or stated.
facts.svg: <polygon points='50,125 170,125 110,30' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='75' y1='80' x2='85' y2='75' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='135' y1='75' x2='145' y2='80' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='105' y1='121' x2='115' y2='129' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><text x='58' y='117' fill='#22c55e' font-size='11'>60</text><text x='148' y='117' fill='#22c55e' font-size='11'>60</text><text x='100' y='58' fill='#22c55e' font-size='11'>60</text>

facts.name: Right angle
facts.rule: A right angle is exactly 90 degrees, and perpendicular lines meet at 90 degrees.
facts.spot: A small square drawn in the corner. Only that square proves it.
facts.trap: A corner that looks square is not square unless the symbol is there or the problem says so. This is the single most exploited trap in PSLE geometry.
facts.svg: <line x1='40' y1='120' x2='190' y2='120' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='70' y1='120' x2='70' y2='30' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='70' y='106' width='14' height='14' fill='none' stroke='#38bdf8' stroke-width='2'/><text x='95' y='100' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='12'>90 degrees</text>

facts.name: Angle sum of a quadrilateral
facts.rule: The four angles inside any four-sided shape add up to 360 degrees.
clue: three angles given in a quadrilateral
facts.trap: Works for any four-sided shape, even a very irregular one. Splitting it into two triangles is the proof and also a useful method.
facts.svg: <polygon points='35,110 80,30 180,45 165,125' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='35' y1='110' x2='180' y2='45' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='55' y='95' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='11'>a</text><text x='82' y='48' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='11'>b</text><text x='160' y='60' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='11'>c</text><text x='150' y='112' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='11'>d</text><text x='30' y='142' fill='currentColor' font-size='11'>a + b + c + d = 360</text>

shapes.title: What each special shape gives you for free
shapes.intro: Naming the shape hands you facts you did not have to work out. If a figure is named, write down what that name guarantees before doing anything else.

rows.gives: Four right angles. All four sides equal. Diagonals cut the corners into two 45 degree halves.
Four right angles. Opposite sides equal. Diagonals are equal in length.
Opposite sides parallel and equal. Opposite angles equal. Neighbouring angles add to 180.
All four sides equal. Opposite angles equal. Diagonals cross at right angles and bisect the angles.
One pair of parallel sides. The two angles on the same slanted side add to 180.
Two equal sides, and the two angles opposite them are equal.
Three equal sides and three angles of 60 degrees.
One angle of 90, so the other two must add to 90.

routine.title: How to attack an angle question

steps.do: Copy the figure if you can, or work lightly on the given one. You will need room to write.
steps.why: A crowded diagram is unreadable by step four.

steps.do: Mark every given: the numbers, the tick marks on equal sides, the arrows on parallel lines, the right-angle squares.
steps.why: Arrows and ticks are the permission slips. Without them you may not use the parallel or isosceles rules.

steps.do: Name the shapes you can see, including ones hidden inside others, and write down what each name gives you.
steps.why: Most of the missing information is not in the numbers, it is in the shape names.

steps.do: Fill in every angle you can reach in one step, writing the reason for each.
steps.why: You rarely see the whole path in advance. Filling in the easy ones reveals it.

steps.do: Look for the letters: F for corresponding, Z for alternate, C for co-interior, X for vertically opposite.
steps.why: Spotting the letter is faster than reasoning about position, and it is reliable once practised.

steps.do: Check the angle you were asked for, and check it is sensible: obtuse angles should look obtuse.
steps.why: A 140 degree answer for an angle that is clearly sharp means an error somewhere, even if the arithmetic was right.

traps.trap: Using a parallel-line rule without parallel lines
traps.fix: Look for the arrowheads. No arrows and no statement means no corresponding, alternate or co-interior.
Same side of the crossing line means they ADD to 180. Opposite sides means they are EQUAL.

traps.trap: Assuming a right angle from the picture
traps.fix: Only the small square counts. Diagrams are not to scale.

traps.trap: Assuming a triangle is isosceles because it looks it
traps.fix: Only tick marks or a written statement count.

traps.trap: Giving a number with no reason
traps.fix: Every line needs its reason in brackets. Reasons carry marks.

traps.trap: Stopping at an angle that is not the one asked for
traps.fix: Circle the required angle on the diagram before you start, so you cannot forget which it is.

traps.trap: Adding the wrong two angles for an exterior angle
traps.fix: Use the two at the far corners, the ones the exterior angle does not touch.
When several triangles overlap, outline the one you are using with your pencil before applying the 180 rule.

strategies.title: Eight ways in when you cannot see the answer
strategies.intro: An angle question is a short argument. If you cannot see the last line, you find any line you can and write it down. Marking one new angle usually reveals the next.

list.name: Chain from what you know
list.when: Always. This is the default and it solves most questions on its own.
list.how: Mark every angle you can get in ONE step from what is already on the diagram. Then look again: new angles have appeared, so more one-step moves are now possible. Repeat until the one you want appears.
list.why: You never have to see the whole route in advance. You only ever have to see the next step, which is far easier.

list.name: Draw a parallel line through the corner
list.when: Two parallel lines with a zigzag, dog-leg or step between them, and an angle at the bend.
list.how: Through the bend, draw a new line parallel to the other two. The angle at the bend is now split into two, and each half sits inside a Z or an F with a line you already know.
list.why: This is the single highest-value trick in PSLE angle work. The bend angle equals the sum of the two outer angles, and without the extra line there is no route at all.

list.name: Whole minus part
list.when: The angle you want is what is left over after other angles are taken away.
list.how: Find the whole angle first: 180 on a straight line, 360 at a point, 360 in a quadrilateral. Subtract the parts you know.
list.why: Often faster than building the angle up, and it uses facts you already have on the page.

list.name: Hunt for the isosceles triangle
list.when: Two sides are marked equal, or two sides are radii of the same circle, or two sides are sides of the same square.
list.how: Equal sides mean equal base angles. Mark both base angles with the same letter immediately, before you calculate anything.
list.why: Two equal angles halve the work, and this is where the information is hidden when a question looks like it has too few numbers.

list.name: Use the exterior angle shortcut
list.when: A side of a triangle is extended and you want the angle outside.
list.how: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles it is not touching. Use it directly instead of finding the third angle and then subtracting from 180.
list.why: It saves one step, and one fewer step is one fewer place to slip.

list.name: Work in the shape you know most about
list.when: A diagram has several triangles and quadrilaterals overlapping.
list.how: Count the known angles inside each shape. Start with the shape where only one is missing.
list.why: You are looking for the shape that is already almost solved, not the one containing the answer.

list.name: Use the named shape's own properties
list.when: The question names a square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, kite or trapezium.
list.how: The name is data. Square and rectangle: every corner 90. Parallelogram: opposite angles equal and neighbouring angles add to 180. Rhombus: all sides equal, so every triangle inside is isosceles, and the diagonals cut the corner angles in half. Isosceles trapezium: the two base angles at each parallel side are equal.
list.why: Pupils read the name and then ignore it. The name is often the only place the missing number comes from.

list.name: Extend a line
list.when: Nothing forms a triangle or a straight line, so no rule applies.
list.how: Extend one of the lines with a ruler until it meets another. You have created a straight line, a triangle, or a pair of vertically opposite angles that you can now use.
list.why: Rules need a shape to sit in. If no rule fits, build the shape the rule needs.

worked.title: Three chains, written the way you should write them
worked.intro: Write the reason in brackets after every line. Method marks live in the reasons, and a chain with no reasons is a chain the marker cannot follow.

list.q: In triangle ABC, angle A is 64 degrees and angle B is 53 degrees. BC is extended to D. Find angle ACD.
steps: angle ACB = 180 − 64 − 53 = 63 degrees (angle sum of a triangle)
angle ACD = 180 − 63 = 117 degrees (angles on a straight line)
list.shortcut: Or in one line: angle ACD = 64 + 53 = 117 degrees (exterior angle of a triangle), which is the same answer with one step fewer.

list.q: Two horizontal lines are parallel. A line steps between them with a bend at P. The angle between the upper line and the upper arm is 35 degrees; between the lower line and the lower arm is 48 degrees. Find the angle at the bend.
steps: Draw a line through P parallel to the two given lines. This splits the bend angle into two parts.
Upper part = 35 degrees (alternate angles, the Z)
Lower part = 48 degrees (alternate angles, the Z)
list.shortcut: Without the extra parallel line there is no route to this answer at all. When you see a bend between parallels, draw it straight away.

list.q: ABCD is a quadrilateral. Angle A and angle B are right angles and angle C is 118 degrees. Triangle CDE is isosceles with DC = DE and angle CDE = 44 degrees. Find angle D of the quadrilateral, and the base angles of the triangle.
steps: angle D = 360 − 90 − 90 − 118 = 62 degrees (angle sum of a quadrilateral)
In triangle CDE, DC = DE so the two base angles are equal (isosceles triangle)
Each base angle = (180 − 44) ÷ 2 = 68 degrees (angle sum of a triangle)
list.shortcut: The word isosceles is the data. Mark the two equal angles with the same letter before you calculate anything.
list.answer: angle D = 62 degrees; base angles 68 degrees each
